overview: Unit 6: identity, body image, role performance, self-esteem, and psychosocial development. Recognize alterations in self and plan respectful, consistent nursing and collaborative care.

topics.title: Alterations in Self: Body Image, Eating & Relationships
Nursing Care for Self-Concept: Trust, Boundaries & Recovery

flashcards.front: “I cannot fulfill my responsibilities as a parent.” Which component deserves exploration?
flashcards.back: Role performance, along with coping, support, and possible effects on self-esteem.

flashcards.front: What supports autonomy in a toddler?
flashcards.back: Safe limited choices and participation matched to ability.

flashcards.front: How can a nurse support industry in a school-age child?
flashcards.back: Teach a manageable skill, allow practice, and praise specific effort and progress.

flashcards.front: Why should an older adult not automatically be assigned a goal of retirement adjustment?
flashcards.back: Roles and priorities are individual; assess what matters to the person rather than infer it from age.

flashcards.front: Define Self-concept
flashcards.back: The person’s overall perception of who they are, shaped through experience.

flashcards.front: Define Personal identity
flashcards.back: The sense of being a unique person with particular values, beliefs, characteristics, and relationships.

flashcards.front: Define Body image
flashcards.back: The mental picture and feelings a person has about their physical self.

flashcards.front: Does a normal-looking body size exclude an eating disorder?
flashcards.back: No. Assess behavior, distress, symptoms, and complications regardless of appearance.

flashcards.front: What does a positive SCOFF result mean?
flashcards.back: Further evaluation is indicated; the screen does not establish a specific diagnosis.

flashcards.front: How should repeated angry behavior be documented?
flashcards.back: Describe observable actions and exact words, context, interventions, and response rather than a stigmatizing label.

flashcards.front: A client discussing body image says they want to die. What changes?
flashcards.back: Immediate safety assessment and the appropriate response take priority over routine body-image teaching.

flashcards.front: Define Body-image disturbance
flashcards.back: Distress or distorted perception related to the physical self, with varying effects on function.

flashcards.front: Define Anorexia nervosa
flashcards.back: An eating disorder involving restriction and associated weight, body-image, and fear-related features requiring comprehensive diagnosis.

flashcards.front: Define Bulimia nervosa
flashcards.back: Recurrent binge eating with compensatory behaviors; diagnosis requires more than an isolated episode.

flashcards.front: What makes feedback more useful than “Good job”?
flashcards.back: It names the actual effort or safe skill and helps the client recognize what worked.

flashcards.front: Does setting limits require withholding essential care?
flashcards.back: No. Maintain safety expectations while continuing appropriate assessment and treatment.

flashcards.front: What should team handoff include after a difficult interaction?
flashcards.back: Observable behavior, context, triggers, interventions, response, safety concerns, and the agreed plan.

flashcards.front: How can self-concept progress be evaluated?
flashcards.back: Through the client’s experience plus specific behavior, participation, coping, safety, and function.

flashcards.front: Define Therapeutic relationship
flashcards.back: A professional, goal-directed relationship focused on the client’s health and well-being.

flashcards.front: Define Empathy
flashcards.back: Recognizing and acknowledging another person’s feelings without assuming identical experience.

flashcards.front: Define Professional boundary
flashcards.back: A limit that protects the purpose, safety, and integrity of the therapeutic relationship.

questions.stem: A client after an amputation says, “I am worried that I can no longer be the parent who takes the children to activities.” Which self-concept component should the nurse explore most directly?
options: Personal identity centered on continuity of core values.
Role performance involving a valued parental responsibility.
Body image centered on the residual limb’s appearance.
Self-esteem centered on the client’s overall sense of worth.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Identity can be shaken by limb loss, but the client is not describing a change in who they are or what they value; the concern is about a specific parenting task.

Correct. The client names a valued parenting responsibility they fear they cannot fulfill, which points most directly to role performance. Identity, body image, and self-esteem may also be affected but are not what the statement centers on.
Incorrect. Body image is often affected after amputation, but the client says nothing about how the limb looks; the worry is about doing a parental role.
Incorrect. Self-esteem may drop when a role is threatened, but that is a possible downstream effect; the statement itself centers on the parenting role.
questions.rationale: The statement centers on fulfilling a parental role. Explore its meaning, available support, and adaptations while also assessing other self-concept concerns. Do not assume the physical change has the same meaning for every client.
questions.takeaway: Use the client’s specific concern to identify the component of self.
questions.hintContent: Distinguish what the client does in relationships from how the body looks.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.

questions.stem: A toddler needs routine care and pushes away the washcloth. Which response should the nurse try first when immediate danger is absent?
options: Explain care and perform it without inviting participation.
Ask a parent to hold and soothe the child during care.
Distract the child with a favorite toy during care.
Offer two appropriate choices and a manageable step.
optionRationales: Incorrect. A simple explanation is appropriate, but doing the care without inviting participation ignores the toddler’s need for autonomy and is likely to increase resistance.
Incorrect. Parental comfort is supportive, but it does not address the toddler’s push for control; limited choices let the child participate while care still happens.
Incorrect. Distraction can help during procedures, but it sidesteps the toddler’s need for autonomy rather than supporting it with real, safe choices.

Correct. Toddlers are working on autonomy. Offering two acceptable choices and a small step the child can do keeps care non-optional while giving control, which addresses the resistance more directly than comfort or distraction alone.
questions.rationale: Toddlers seek independence. Safe limited choices and manageable participation can support autonomy without making essential care optional. Use concrete language and assess the child’s actual development.
questions.takeaway: Support autonomy with safe choices that are genuinely available.
questions.hintContent: Choose participation matched to development while preserving the care goal.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.

questions.stem: A school-age child is learning a new self-care skill. Which actions support industry and self-esteem? Select all that apply.
options: Break the task into achievable steps.
Compare performance publicly with faster children.
Praise a specific effort or correctly performed step.
Allow time for practice with appropriate assistance.
Take over permanently after the first error.
optionRationales: Correct. Manageable practice supports competence.
Incorrect. Public comparison can create shame and inferiority.
Correct. Specific feedback helps the child recognize success.
Correct. Practice supports mastery.
Incorrect. This removes the opportunity to learn and adapt.
questions.rationale: School-age children develop competence through achievable work and practice. Specific encouragement and appropriate support strengthen mastery. Public comparison and unnecessary takeover can undermine confidence.
questions.takeaway: Build competence through practice and specific feedback.
questions.hintContent: Select actions that create a realistic experience of mastery.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.

questions.stem: An older adult says that mentoring younger neighbors gives life meaning. Which developmental task is most directly reflected by this activity?
options: Generativity expressed through contribution to younger people.
Integrity expressed through acceptance of one’s whole life.
Intimacy expressed through close and trusting relationships.
Industry expressed through mastering new skills and tasks.
optionRationales: Correct. Mentoring younger people is a classic expression of generativity: contributing to the next generation. An older adult can continue this role while also working on integrity through life review.
Incorrect. Integrity is the expected task of older adulthood, but it centers on life review and acceptance; the activity described is contributing to younger people, which is generativity.
Incorrect. Mentoring involves relationships, but intimacy centers on close, committed bonds; guiding the next generation reflects generativity.
Incorrect. Mentoring may involve skills, but industry is the school-age task of mastery and competence; the meaning here comes from contributing to others.
questions.rationale: Developmental tasks are guides rather than rigid age boxes. Mentoring reflects contribution and generativity, and an older adult may continue this meaningful role while also engaging in life review and integrity.
questions.takeaway: Developmental themes can overlap across ages.
questions.hintContent: Identify the meaning of the activity rather than assigning a task solely by age.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.

questions.stem: A client says, “Since surgery, I do not feel like myself.” Which questions support individualized assessment? Select all that apply.
options: “What changes feel most important to you?”
“Which roles or activities would you most like to regain?”
“You should be grateful; why are you upset?”
“What has helped you cope with difficult changes before?”
“Who would you like involved in these conversations?”
optionRationales: Correct. This explores the client’s meaning.
Correct. This identifies valued function and goals.
Incorrect. This judges the client’s response.
Correct. This identifies strengths.
Correct. This respects support preferences.
questions.rationale: Self-concept assessment includes identity, roles, body image, coping, and chosen supports. Open questions allow the person’s experience to guide care. Gratitude-based criticism can suppress disclosure and trust.
questions.takeaway: Explore meaning, strengths, and preferred support.
questions.hintContent: Favor questions that gather the person’s perspective without prescribing the emotion they should have.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.

questions.stem: A client seeking help for eating concerns reports recurrent vomiting, very limited intake, palpitations, and a near-fainting episode. The client says, “I do not look underweight, so I cannot be medically ill.” Which problem is the nurse’s priority concern?
options: Body-image disturbance linked to distorted self-perception.
Knowledge deficit about the health risks of frequent purging.
Potential physiologic instability from restriction and purging.
Ineffective coping related to emotional distress around food.
optionRationales: Incorrect. The client’s view of their body is a real concern, but palpitations and near-fainting suggest possible electrolyte or cardiac problems, which take priority over psychosocial needs.
Incorrect. The client does misunderstand the risks, and teaching will be needed, but physical warning signs must be assessed before education.

Correct. Recurrent vomiting, very low intake, palpitations, and near-fainting point to possible fluid, electrolyte, or cardiac instability regardless of body size. Physiologic safety comes before body-image, coping, or teaching needs.
Incorrect. Coping problems likely underlie the behavior, but they are a longer-term focus; current physical symptoms make physiologic instability the priority.
questions.rationale: The current physical symptoms suggest possible medical instability, including fluid or electrolyte complications, regardless of body size. This priority hypothesis requires prompt physiologic assessment and evaluation; screening and body-image work do not replace immediate safety care.
questions.takeaway: Physical warning signs take priority over assumptions based on appearance.
questions.hintContent: Use the physiologic symptoms rather than a stereotype of an eating disorder.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A client has two affirmative responses on an appropriately administered SCOFF screen. Which interpretation should guide the nurse?
options: A confirmed disorder requiring its specific treatment protocol.
A positive screen warranting further assessment and referral.
A sign of risk best handled with nutrition teaching first.
A borderline result to rescreen at the next routine visit.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Two affirmative answers do raise real concern, but a screen cannot diagnose a disorder or set treatment; that requires a full evaluation.

Correct. Two or more affirmative SCOFF responses is a referral threshold. The result raises concern, so the nurse assesses safety and physical findings and coordinates further evaluation, without treating the screen as a diagnosis.
Incorrect. Nutrition teaching may be part of later care, but a positive screen first calls for further assessment and referral; teaching alone may miss a serious disorder.
Incorrect. Rescreening is reasonable when results are unclear, but two affirmative answers meet the referral threshold, so waiting delays needed evaluation.
questions.rationale: The course identifies two or more affirmative responses as a referral threshold. A positive screen raises concern but does not determine diagnosis, severity, or treatment. Assess safety and physical findings and coordinate evaluation.
questions.takeaway: A screening threshold prompts assessment; it does not complete diagnosis.
questions.hintContent: Separate the role of a screen from diagnostic and treatment decisions.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.

questions.stem: Which statements about eating-related concerns are appropriate for a nurse to use? Select all that apply.
options: Concerning eating behaviors can occur at different body sizes.
Avoidant restrictive intake always reflects a desire to be thin.
Recurrent binge eating with compensatory behaviors requires comprehensive evaluation.
Nonfood ingestion should be assessed for associated hazards.
A negative brief screen eliminates the need to assess concerning symptoms.
optionRationales: Correct. Appearance alone cannot exclude a disorder.
Incorrect. Avoidance may involve sensory issues, fear, or low interest.
Correct. The pattern raises concern but diagnosis needs full assessment.
Correct. Pica can create health risks requiring evaluation.
Incorrect. Clinical findings can warrant evaluation despite a negative screen.
questions.rationale: Eating-related presentations vary. Assess behavior, distress, function, and physical risk rather than relying on body size or a brief screen alone. Restrictive intake can have mechanisms beyond body-image concerns.
questions.takeaway: Assess the pattern and risk without stereotypes.
questions.hintContent: Judge each claim by whether it overgeneralizes from appearance, screening, or one mechanism.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.

questions.stem: While discussing altered appearance, a client says, “There is no point in living now.” What is the nurse’s priority response?
options: Assess self-harm thoughts and immediate safety directly.
Explore appearance concerns before deciding about risk assessment.
Arrange counseling and continue the scheduled teaching session.
Reassure about recovery and redirect toward short-term goals.
optionRationales: Correct. The statement raises a potential safety concern requiring direct assessment and protocol-based action.
Incorrect. The possible self-harm meaning should not wait for an extended body-image discussion.
Incorrect. Routine follow-up is insufficient when immediate risk is possible.
Incorrect. Reassurance alone does not assess the safety concern.
questions.rationale: Hopelessness and a statement about not living require direct safety assessment and an appropriate response. Maintain a calm nonjudgmental approach and obtain support according to protocol. Routine body-image exercises follow immediate safety care.
questions.takeaway: A possible self-harm disclosure changes the priority.
questions.hintContent: Respond to the safety meaning of the statement before the original teaching topic.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.

questions.stem: A school nurse develops a program supporting body image and self-esteem. Which actions fit the course guidance? Select all that apply.
options: Address appearance-based teasing and cyberbullying.
Use public weigh-ins as the main motivational event.
Offer enjoyable inclusive physical activities.
Use materials representing diverse bodies and abilities.
Praise effort, skills, and personal strengths.
optionRationales: Correct. This supports a safer social environment.
Incorrect. Public measurements can increase shame.
Correct. Participation need not depend on appearance or competition.
Correct. Inclusive representation supports belonging.
Correct. This avoids equating worth with appearance.
questions.rationale: The source emphasizes body-positive environments, prevention of teasing, inclusive media, enjoyable activity, and avoiding public measurements. Support competence and belonging rather than appearance-based comparison.
questions.takeaway: Prevention should reduce shame and expand participation.
questions.hintContent: Select actions supporting inclusion rather than public comparison.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.

questions.stem: A client says, “You promised to return after lunch, but no one came. I cannot trust this team.” Which response should the nurse make first?
options: “I am sorry. The unit got very busy today.”
“Let me ask the charge nurse to talk with you.”
“I will check back with you at 3 o’clock.”
“We missed follow-up. Let us address your need.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. An apology helps, but adding the workload explanation sounds like an excuse and shifts focus away from the client’s unmet need.
Incorrect. Involving the charge nurse may be appropriate later, but handing off the concern first avoids accountability; the nurse can acknowledge the lapse and act now.
Incorrect. A specific, realistic commitment builds trust, but it postpones the unmet need and does not acknowledge the missed follow-up.
Correct. Honestly owning the missed follow-up and acting on the unmet need right away restores trust better than an excuse, a handoff, or a future promise alone.
questions.rationale: Trust is supported by honest acknowledgment, reliable follow-through, and realistic commitments. Defensiveness or impossible promises can worsen the relationship. Assess the unmet need and communicate a feasible plan.
questions.takeaway: Repair trust with acknowledgment and concrete follow-through.
questions.hintContent: Choose a response that is honest and focused on the client’s need.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: After practicing a transfer, which feedback best supports a client’s self-efficacy?
options: “You completed that transfer using the safe technique.”
“Great job! You did really well with that today.”
“You did that transfer better than you did yesterday.”
“Keep practicing, and this will get easier for you.”
optionRationales: Correct. Specific feedback that names what the client did correctly builds self-efficacy through recognized mastery. General praise, comparison, and future encouragement are supportive but less tied to the client’s actual success.
Incorrect. Praise is encouraging, but it is general and does not tell the client which skill was done well, so it builds less confidence from mastery.
Incorrect. Noting progress is supportive, but it centers on comparison rather than naming the safe technique the client used.
Incorrect. Encouraging practice is reasonable, but it looks ahead instead of recognizing the success the client just achieved.
questions.rationale: Specific feedback helps a person recognize what they did successfully and build confidence through mastery. Avoid comparison, dismissal, or overgeneralizing one performance into an unsupported independence claim.
questions.takeaway: Name the actual safe action when reinforcing progress.
questions.hintContent: Look for accurate feedback tied to performance rather than broad praise.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A team plans care for a client who becomes distressed when different staff give conflicting expectations. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Communicate a consistent agreed plan among staff.
Describe triggers and effective responses objectively in handoff.
Withhold necessary symptom assessment until behavior improves.
Use calm respectful limits and available choices.
Debrief staff responses to improve consistency and prevent burnout.
optionRationales: Correct. This reduces contradictory messages.
Correct. Specific information supports continuity.
Incorrect. Boundaries must not replace appropriate clinical care.
Correct. This maintains safety and autonomy.
Correct. Reflection can support professional care.
questions.rationale: Consistency, objective communication, calm boundaries, and team support can improve the therapeutic environment. Limits are not punishment, and a behavioral concern does not remove the need for appropriate medical assessment and treatment.
questions.takeaway: Consistent boundaries should support care rather than withhold it.
questions.hintContent: Select actions preserving both safety and appropriate treatment.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A client says a prescribed antidepressant should “fix my whole personality and all my relationships.” Which response is most accurate?
options: “Many people notice changes within a few weeks.”
“It targets symptoms within a broader treatment plan.”
“Be sure to take it exactly as it was prescribed.”
“Your provider can explain what this drug treats.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is true about onset, but it does not correct the belief that the drug will fix personality and relationships.
Correct. The client expects the drug to fix everything. Explaining that it targets symptoms as one part of a broader plan corrects the misconception directly and sets realistic expectations.
Incorrect. Adherence teaching is important, but it does not address the client’s unrealistic expectation of what the drug can do.
Incorrect. The provider can add detail, but medication teaching is within the nurse’s role, and deferring leaves the misconception uncorrected.
questions.rationale: Medication may address diagnosed symptoms such as depression or anxiety, but it is not a universal remedy for self-concept or relationships. Teach the actual purpose, monitor response, and support the coordinated plan.
questions.takeaway: Explain medication as one part of symptom-focused coordinated care.
questions.hintContent: Avoid claims that a treatment either solves everything or has no possible role.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A client is learning device care but becomes tearful and says, “I cannot face looking at it yet.” No immediate care emergency is present. What should the nurse do first?
options: Continue the demonstration while offering reassurance.
Ask a family member to learn the device care for now.
Explore distress and agree on a manageable next step.
Postpone all teaching until the client says they are ready.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reassurance is kind and the skill is needed, but continuing as planned skips assessing the client’s distress and may overwhelm learning.
Incorrect. A support person may help, but shifting teaching without the client’s input bypasses their preferences and their own adaptation.
Correct. Exploring what the distress means and agreeing on a small next step respects body-image adaptation while keeping necessary learning moving.
Incorrect. Respecting readiness is reasonable, but stopping all teaching without a plan delays needed self-care skills; a manageable step keeps progress going.
questions.rationale: Body-image adaptation and skill learning may progress at different rates. Assess the meaning of the distress, preserve necessary care, and agree on a feasible next step with support. Immediate danger is absent, so coercive speed is not justified.
questions.takeaway: Support gradual participation according to assessed readiness.
questions.hintContent: Use the absence of an emergency to choose a respectful assessment and next step.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A 4-year-old scheduled for a blood draw keeps asking, “What is that for?” about the tourniquet and bandages. The procedure must occur today. Which action should the nurse take first to support the child’s developmental needs?
options: Give a short, honest explanation right before the draw begins.
Let the child touch the supplies and “practice” on a stuffed animal.
Let the child choose which arm to use for the blood draw.
Have a parent hold and comfort the child during the draw.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Brief, honest explanations given close to the procedure fit preschoolers, but words alone answer the child’s questions less well than hands-on play with the actual supplies.
Correct. Preschoolers learn through hands-on play and questions. Handling safe supplies and rehearsing on a toy answers the child’s questions concretely and builds initiative before the procedure.
Incorrect. A limited choice supports control, but it does not answer the child’s questions about the equipment; play rehearsal addresses the curiosity directly.
Incorrect. Parental comfort reduces fear during the draw, but it does not meet the child’s present need to explore and understand the supplies.
questions.rationale: Preschool children develop initiative through exploration, play, and questions. Letting the child handle safe equipment and rehearse on a toy gives a developmentally appropriate explanation and a sense of participation. Limited choices and parental comfort also help, but they do not answer the child’s questions the way play does. The procedure itself is not optional, and explanations should be concrete and brief, given with enough time for the child to explore.
questions.takeaway: For preschoolers, use play and simple explanation to support initiative within necessary care.
questions.hintContent: Match the intervention to initiative: exploration, play, and questions.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old with a new insulin pump has stopped going to swim practice and says, “Everyone is going to stare at this thing.” Which response should the nurse make first?
options: “Lots of teens with diabetes wear pumps and still swim.”
“Let me review again how the pump keeps your blood glucose controlled.”
“Would you like to meet another teen who uses a pump?”
“What worries you most about how your teammates might react?”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is true and meant to reassure, but it skips over the teen’s specific fear and can feel dismissive.
Incorrect. Teaching about the pump is useful, but the teen is voicing a peer and self-image concern, not a knowledge gap.
Incorrect. Peer support can help adolescents, but offering it before learning what the teen fears is intervening before assessing.

Correct. Adolescents are forming identity and care deeply about peers. Exploring the specific fear first lets the nurse and teen plan together, such as disclosure choices or managing the device during swimming.
questions.rationale: Adolescents are working on identity, and appearance, peer belonging, and privacy may matter greatly. Withdrawing from a valued activity because of peer reactions is a self-concept concern, not a knowledge deficit about the device. The nurse first explores what the adolescent fears, then problem-solves collaboratively, such as options for disclosure, peer support, or managing the device around swimming per the diabetes plan. General reassurance or jumping to solutions before understanding the fear weakens engagement.
questions.takeaway: With adolescents, explore the peer and identity concern directly before teaching or problem-solving.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether the stated problem is missing information or the meaning of being seen with a device.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.

questions.stem: A former competitive runner recovering from a knee reconstruction says, “In my head I am still the athlete I want to be, but now I am just someone who limps around with a cane.” Which interpretation best guides the nurse’s assessment?
options: The client’s public self has replaced the client’s personal identity.
The client is in denial about how serious the injury really is.
A gap between the client’s real and ideal self may be causing distress.
The client is showing body-image distress about using a cane.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Others’ views may matter to an athlete, but the client is contrasting how they see themselves with who they want to be, not public versus personal identity.
Incorrect. Denial is common after injury, but this client openly acknowledges the limp and cane, so the statement does not suggest denial.
Correct. The client contrasts who they want to be (the athlete) with how they now see themselves, describing a real-ideal self gap that can cause distress and threaten identity.
Incorrect. The cane may affect body image, but the client’s distress is about identity as an athlete, which the real-ideal self gap explains more fully.
questions.rationale: The real self is how the person believes they are, and the ideal self is who they want to be. This client describes a large gap between the two, which can produce distress and threaten identity. The nurse acknowledges the loss and explores what remains meaningful and what adaptation might matter now. These concepts describe perceptions, not an objective measure of worth, and the concern is broader than appearance alone.
questions.takeaway: A large real–ideal self gap signals distress to explore, not a label to assign.
questions.hintContent: Real self is “how I am now”; ideal self is “who I want to be”; public self is “how others see me.”
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.

questions.stem: A nurse who highly values independence feels frustrated that an older adult recovering from pneumonia lets an adult daughter help with bathing and make many daily decisions. The client is medically able to do more and says this arrangement is normal in the family. What should the nurse do first?
options: Examine own values about independence, then ask about the client’s preferences.
Encourage the client to try bathing with standby help to build strength.
Teach the daughter ways to promote the client’s independence at home.
Ask the client which self-care tasks the client would like to do alone.
optionRationales: Correct. The nurse first recognizes that their own value on independence is shaping the reaction, then asks what the client wants. This prevents imposing the nurse’s values and builds goals around the client’s chosen family roles.
Incorrect. Building strength supports recovery, but pushing independent bathing reflects the nurse’s values before learning what the client wants.
Incorrect. Family teaching can be useful, but redirecting the daughter assumes the arrangement is a problem the client has not identified.
Incorrect. Asking about preferences is a good step, but this question still frames the goal as doing tasks alone, reflecting the nurse’s value on independence that should be examined first.
questions.rationale: Nurses bring their own beliefs about independence and family into care, and these can distort interpretation. A client’s values may differ from the nurse’s without being unhealthy. The first step is to notice that reaction and then ask what the client wants, including which tasks the client hopes to keep doing. Goals can then support safe recovery and the client’s chosen family roles.
questions.takeaway: Check your own values before labeling a client’s different preference as a problem.
questions.hintContent: Notice whose values are driving the conclusion that something is wrong.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client receiving palliative care says, “Lately I keep thinking back over my life. Some of it I am proud of, and some of it I regret.” The client denies hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm. Which response best supports this developmental stage?
options: “It sounds like you have lived a full and meaningful life.”
“Would you like me to ask the chaplain to visit with you?”
“Have you shared these thoughts with anyone in your family?”
“Tell me about the parts you are proud of and the parts you regret.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is warm, but it offers a conclusion for the client and passes over the regrets the client raised.
Incorrect. Spiritual care may help in palliative care, but referring the client elsewhere first misses the chance to support the life review now.
Incorrect. Family support matters, but this question shifts focus away from the client’s reflection instead of inviting it.

Correct. Older adulthood involves life review and integrity versus despair. Inviting the client to share both pride and regret supports reflection directly, rather than concluding, referring, or redirecting.
questions.rationale: Older adulthood involves life review and the tension between integrity and despair. Inviting the client to share both proud moments and regrets supports reflection and acknowledges the person’s contributions. Offering a conclusion, referring right away, or shifting the focus to others can leave the client alone with unresolved feelings. If hopelessness or self-harm cues emerged, direct safety assessment would take priority.
questions.takeaway: Support integrity by inviting life review rather than redirecting it.
questions.hintContent: Which response lets the client continue the reflection they started?
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old client with a new colostomy says, “I do not know how I will ever date again.” Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Acknowledge the concern and ask what worries the client most about dating.
Tell the client to wait until fully healed before thinking about relationships.
Offer private time to discuss questions about intimacy and sexuality.
Advise the client never to tell future partners about the ostomy.
Offer a referral to an ostomy nurse or peer support group if the client wishes.
Change the subject to pouch-emptying steps because physical care comes first.
optionRationales: Correct. Exploring the specific concern respects its meaning to the client.
Incorrect. Postponing the concern dismisses a central developmental need for intimacy.
Correct. Privacy allows sensitive questions about intimacy to be raised.
Incorrect. Disclosure is the client’s decision; a blanket rule imposes the nurse’s values and may increase shame.
Correct. Specialty and peer resources can support adaptation when the client wants them.
Incorrect. No urgent physical need is described, and avoiding the topic signals that it is not acceptable to discuss.
questions.rationale: Young adulthood emphasizes intimacy and connection, so a change in appearance or body function can threaten relationships and future plans. The nurse acknowledges the concern, explores its meaning, and offers a private space for sensitive questions. Referrals to specialty and peer resources are offered as choices, not imposed. Dismissing, delaying, or redirecting the concern can deepen shame and isolation.
questions.takeaway: For young adults, treat intimacy concerns as a legitimate part of the care plan.
questions.hintContent: Intimacy versus isolation: which actions keep connection and choice open?
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old construction supervisor who coaches a youth baseball team is in rehabilitation after a spinal cord injury and says, “I used to be the one who taught everybody.” Which nursing actions support this client’s self-concept? Select all that apply.
options: Ask which contributions and roles matter most to the client now.
Plan for the client to accept that work and coaching roles have ended.
Explore adapted ways to keep mentoring, such as teaching strategy from the dugout.
Have family make care decisions so the client can focus on rest.
Coordinate with rehabilitation and social work about workplace adaptations.
Involve the client in setting rehabilitation goals and schedules.
optionRationales: Correct. Assessing valued roles guides individualized goals.
Incorrect. This assumes loss of all roles instead of exploring adaptation.
Correct. Adapting a valued role preserves contribution and generativity.
Incorrect. Removing decisions undermines autonomy and a strength the client still has.
Correct. Interprofessional resources can help restore work-related roles.
Correct. Participation in decisions preserves control and self-esteem.
questions.rationale: Middle adulthood often centers on generativity, which is contributing through work, family, mentoring, or community. A new disability can disrupt those roles and threaten purpose. The nurse assesses which contributions matter, helps adapt them, and coordinates practical resources. A client who needs physical help can still lead decisions and mentor others.
questions.takeaway: Preserve valued contributions by adapting roles rather than assuming they are lost.
questions.hintContent: Generativity is about contributing; look for options that keep the client contributing.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old is admitted for several days of IV antibiotics, and the parents cannot stay overnight. Which nursing action is the priority to support the infant’s psychosocial development?
options: Place a familiar blanket or toy from home in the infant’s crib.
Encourage the parents to call the unit for updates each day.
Assign consistent caregivers and respond promptly to the infant’s cries.
Cluster care so the infant has longer periods of uninterrupted rest.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Comfort objects can soothe, but they do not replace consistent, responsive caregivers, which are central to building trust.
Incorrect. Keeping parents informed is helpful, but it supports the parents more than it meets the infant’s direct need for responsive care.

Correct. Infancy centers on trust versus mistrust. When parents cannot stay, consistent caregivers who respond promptly to cries give the predictability the infant needs; comfort objects and parent updates are helpful additions.
Incorrect. Clustering care supports rest, a physical need, but it does not address the infant’s psychosocial need for consistent, responsive caregivers.
questions.rationale: Infancy centers on trust versus mistrust, which is supported by consistent, responsive care. When parents cannot be present, assigning consistent caregivers and comforting the infant promptly provide predictability. Keeping parents informed and encouraging familiar routines or comfort objects can also help. Developmental frameworks describe needs; one hospitalization does not determine a permanent outcome, but responsive care still matters.
questions.takeaway: Infants build trust through consistent, responsive caregiving.
questions.hintContent: Trust grows from predictability and prompt comfort.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.

questions.stem: A client with anorexia nervosa began a nutrition-restoration plan 2 days ago. Which finding requires the nurse’s immediate follow-up?
options: States, “I feel too full after every meal.”
Serum phosphorus of 1.8 mg/dL.
Weight up 0.5 kg (1.1 lb) since admission.
Reports feeling cold in the room.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Early fullness is common as intake increases and is worth noting, but it is uncomfortable rather than dangerous.
Correct. Low phosphorus soon after nutrition restarts suggests refeeding syndrome, which can cause cardiac and respiratory complications.
Incorrect. Weight is monitored closely during refeeding, but a small gain over 2 days is expected and is not an immediate threat.
Incorrect. Cold intolerance is common with low body weight and needs comfort measures, but it does not signal acute danger the way low phosphorus does.
questions.rationale: When nutrition is restarted after severe restriction, refeeding syndrome can develop, marked by drops in phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium. A phosphorus of 1.8 mg/dL is below the usual reference range of about 2.5–4.5 mg/dL and can lead to dysrhythmias, weakness, and respiratory compromise. The nurse should promptly report the value and follow the monitoring and escalation plan. Electrolyte replacement and changes to the feeding plan are interprofessional decisions, not something the nurse designs alone.
questions.takeaway: Watch phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium closely in the first days of refeeding.
questions.hintContent: Ask which finding signals a physiologic complication of restarting nutrition.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A client with an eating disorder reports self-induced vomiting several times a day. Which assessment finding should the nurse report first?
options: Fine, downy hair on the arms and back.
Reports of fatigue by late afternoon.
Expressed fear of gaining weight.
Serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Lanugo can occur with eating disorders but does not create immediate risk.
Incorrect. Fatigue warrants assessment but is less urgent than a dangerous electrolyte value.
Incorrect. Fear of weight gain is an important psychological feature but not an immediate physiologic threat.
Correct. Hypokalemia from repeated vomiting can cause life-threatening dysrhythmias.
questions.rationale: Repeated purging causes potassium loss, and hypokalemia can trigger dangerous cardiac dysrhythmias. A potassium of 2.9 mEq/L is below the usual reference range of about 3.5–5.0 mEq/L and needs prompt reporting and cardiac assessment according to protocol. Lanugo, fatigue, and fear of weight gain matter for the overall picture but do not pose the same immediate risk. In priority questions, physiologic instability comes before long-term psychological goals.
questions.takeaway: Purging plus low potassium means dysrhythmia risk; report it first.
questions.hintContent: Which finding could cause harm in the next few hours?
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A client reports eating very large amounts of food in a short time several times a week, feeling out of control and ashamed afterward. The client denies vomiting, laxative use, fasting, or excessive exercise. Which pattern should the nurse recognize as most consistent with these findings?
options: A possible binge-eating presentation needing further evaluation.
A possible bulimia presentation needing further evaluation.
A possible anorexia presentation needing further evaluation.
A possible avoidant restrictive intake presentation needing further evaluation.
optionRationales: Correct. Recurrent distressing binges without regular compensatory behavior fit a binge-eating pattern.
Incorrect. Bulimia involves binges followed by compensatory behaviors, which the client denies.
Incorrect. Anorexia involves restriction with weight and body-image concerns, not recurrent binges.
Incorrect. Avoidant restrictive intake involves limiting food, often from sensory aversion or fear, not bingeing.
questions.rationale: Binge-eating disorder involves recurrent distressing binge episodes without the regular compensatory behaviors that characterize bulimia. The key cue separating the two is the absence of vomiting, laxatives, fasting, or excessive exercise. The nurse recognizes the pattern and supports referral, because diagnosis requires comprehensive professional evaluation. Shame is common, so a nonjudgmental approach helps keep the client engaged.
questions.takeaway: Binges without regular compensation point toward binge-eating, not bulimia.
questions.hintContent: Look for what the client does, or does not do, after a binge.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old has lost weight after eating only a few soft foods since a choking episode. The child expresses no concern about body shape. Which statement by a nursing student indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “Fear of choking can drive restrictive eating in children.”
“We should ask which textures the child avoids and why.”
“The weight loss means this child must have anorexia nervosa.”
“Growth and nutrition need evaluation even without body-image concerns.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This statement is accurate; fear of consequences can drive avoidant restrictive intake.
Incorrect. This statement is accurate; exploring textures and fears is part of assessment.
Correct. Weight loss alone does not establish anorexia; restriction here is driven by fear, not body-image concerns.
Incorrect. This statement is accurate; restriction can harm growth whatever its cause.
questions.rationale: Avoidant restrictive food intake can stem from sensory avoidance, fear of consequences such as choking, or low interest in eating, and it is not simply a desire for thinness. This child has no body-shape concern, which argues against assuming anorexia. Restriction can still threaten growth and nutrition, so evaluation is needed. The student who equates weight loss with anorexia needs teaching about distinguishing mechanisms.
questions.takeaway: Restriction without body-image concern suggests mechanisms other than anorexia.
questions.hintContent: Find the statement that jumps from one finding to a diagnosis.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.

questions.stem: A client recovering from facial burns says, “I do not want my partner to see me like this. He gets angry when things go wrong.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Reassure the client that the grafts will look better as they heal.
Ask privately whether the client feels safe with the partner at home.
Encourage the partner to visit often so the client gets used to being seen.
Teach the client about camouflage makeup options for after discharge.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reassurance about appearance skips assessment of a possible safety concern.
Correct. The reference to the partner’s anger is a cue that requires private safety assessment.
Incorrect. Increasing contact before assessing safety could expose the client to harm.
Incorrect. Adaptation teaching may help later but does not address the possible risk.
questions.rationale: A statement such as “I do not want my partner to see me” may reflect body-image distress, a need for privacy, or a relationship safety concern. The added cue about the partner’s anger means the nurse should not assume the issue is appearance alone. Asking privately about safety at home comes first, then follows the facility’s protocol if risk is identified. Body-image support and adaptation teaching can continue once safety is clarified.
questions.takeaway: When a body-image statement includes a relationship risk cue, assess safety first.
questions.hintContent: Do not assume one cause; notice the cue about the partner.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.

questions.stem: A caregiver reports that a 3-year-old has repeatedly eaten peeling paint chips and soil over the past 2 months, even after being redirected. Which interpretation should guide the nurse’s next step?
options: Persistent nonfood eating needs assessment for hazards such as lead exposure.
Mouthing objects is expected at this age, so reassurance is the main need.
The behavior shows the child is not receiving enough calories at meals.
Removing access to paint chips and soil is the main need at this point.
optionRationales: Correct. Repeatedly eating paint chips and soil for months is pica, not ordinary mouthing, and can expose the child to lead and other hazards. The history needs reporting so exposure and causes can be evaluated.
Incorrect. Some mouthing is normal in young children, but repeatedly eating paint and soil for 2 months is beyond expected behavior and carries real hazards.
Incorrect. Nutritional deficits such as iron deficiency can be linked to pica, but assuming low calories skips assessment for lead exposure and other causes.
Incorrect. Removing access is a reasonable safety step, but the child may already be exposed to lead, so assessment is still needed.
questions.rationale: Pica is the persistent eating of nonfood substances beyond what is developmentally and culturally expected. Repeatedly eating peeling paint chips over months is not ordinary mouthing and can expose the child to lead and other hazards. The nurse should report the history so exposure and associated causes can be evaluated. Reassurance or simply removing access would miss a potentially serious health risk that may already exist.
questions.takeaway: Persistent nonfood eating needs assessment for associated hazards such as lead exposure.
questions.hintContent: Compare the behavior with what is developmentally expected and consider what was eaten.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A client has raised their voice at staff several times this shift. Which documentation entries are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: “Client stated, ‘Nobody here listens to me,’ in a raised voice at 1400.”
“Client is manipulative and seeking attention.”
“Offered quiet room at 1410; client accepted, and voice lowered within 10 minutes.”
“Client was difficult and uncooperative all shift.”
“Client likely has borderline personality disorder based on today’s outburst.”
“Client walked to the nurses’ station three times in 30 minutes asking about discharge.”
optionRationales: Correct. Exact words, time, and observable behavior are objective.
Incorrect. This is a stigmatizing label that assumes motive instead of describing behavior.
Correct. Recording the intervention and the client’s response supports consistent care.
Incorrect. Vague judgmental terms do not describe what actually happened.
Incorrect. A single episode does not establish a personality disorder, and the nurse should not chart a diagnosis from it.
Correct. Frequency and specific behavior are objective, useful data.
questions.rationale: Documentation should describe observable behavior, exact words, context, interventions, and the client’s response. Labels such as “manipulative” or “difficult” stigmatize the client and do not tell the next nurse what happened or what helped. A personality disorder is an enduring pattern that requires comprehensive assessment, so one angry interaction cannot establish it. Objective entries support a consistent, therapeutic team plan.
questions.takeaway: Chart behavior, words, interventions, and response, not labels or motives.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each entry describes something seen or heard, or a judgment about the person.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse in a college health clinic is using the SCOFF questionnaire with a student who reports worry about eating. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Use the questionnaire’s authorized wording in a private setting.
Explain that the purpose is to understand what support may help.
Rephrase the items casually in the nurse’s own words to ease tension.
Arrange further evaluation if two or more responses are affirmative.
Tell the student that two affirmative responses confirm an eating disorder.
Document the tool used, the result, the context, and the follow-up plan.
optionRationales: Correct. Validated tools rely on authorized wording, and privacy supports honest answers.
Correct. Explaining the purpose reduces fear and supports engagement.
Incorrect. Improvised wording invalidates the screen and its scoring.
Correct. Two or more affirmative answers indicate a need for further evaluation.
Incorrect. SCOFF is a screen; a positive result does not diagnose a specific disorder.
Correct. Specific documentation supports follow-up without labeling the student.
questions.rationale: SCOFF is a brief screen that identifies a need for further assessment; it does not diagnose. Using the authorized wording in a private setting preserves validity and dignity. Two or more affirmative answers should lead to further evaluation and attention to medical and psychological safety. Documentation should record the tool, result, context, and follow-up rather than a diagnostic label.
questions.takeaway: Administer SCOFF as written and in private, and treat a positive result as a reason to evaluate further.
questions.hintContent: Separate administering and following up on a screen from making a diagnosis.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.

questions.stem: A client who had a mastectomy yesterday has avoided looking at the incision and says she feels “less like a woman.” Which task can the RN delegate to the unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?
options: Assess the client’s feelings about her changed appearance.
Evaluate the client’s readiness to look at the incision.
Assist the client with morning hygiene while maintaining privacy.
Teach the client about breast prosthesis and reconstruction options.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Psychosocial assessment requires RN judgment and cannot be delegated.
Incorrect. Evaluating readiness is an assessment and evaluation task for the RN.
Correct. Assisting with hygiene while preserving privacy is within UAP scope and supports dignity.
Incorrect. Teaching about treatment options is an RN responsibility.
questions.rationale: Assessment, teaching, and evaluation require RN clinical judgment and cannot be delegated. Assisting with hygiene for a stable client is within UAP scope, and protecting privacy during that care supports the client’s dignity and body image. The RN can ask the UAP to report observations, such as distress or reluctance to view the incision. The RN remains responsible for exploring the meaning of the change and planning support.
questions.takeaway: Delegate routine care that preserves dignity; keep psychosocial assessment, teaching, and evaluation with the RN.
questions.hintContent: Assessment, teaching, and evaluation stay with the RN.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client stands at the nurses’ station shouting about wanting to go outside to smoke, and other clients are watching. The client has made no threats and has no weapon. Which response should the nurse make first?
options: “Smoking is not allowed on the unit. Please return to your room.”
“Other clients are getting upset. Please lower your voice right now.”
“I can ask the provider about a nicotine patch to help with cravings.”
“I want to help. Let us talk in the quiet room or here once voices lower.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stating the rule is a clear limit, but it ignores the client’s concern and offers no choice, which can escalate frustration.
Incorrect. Asking for a lower voice sets a limit, but focusing on other clients can feel shaming and does not acknowledge the client’s need.
Incorrect. Nicotine replacement may help later, but jumping to a solution before calming the situation is mistimed and does not set a limit.
Correct. A therapeutic limit calmly acknowledges the concern, states the expectation, and offers choices. Moving to a quieter space protects the client’s dignity and other clients’ comfort.
questions.rationale: Therapeutic limits state the expectation calmly, acknowledge the person’s concern, and offer available choices. Rules stated without acknowledgment, or limits that focus on others, can feel punitive and escalate behavior, while solutions offered before de-escalation are mistimed. A private, quieter space also protects the client’s dignity and other clients’ comfort. If danger develops, the nurse obtains help and follows the response plan rather than managing it alone.
questions.takeaway: Set limits calmly with a stated expectation and real choices, without threats or bargaining.
questions.hintContent: Look for the response that keeps both the limit and the relationship.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A client known for angry outbursts is shouting at staff and reports new chest pain rated 8/10. A coworker says, “Ignore the requests until the yelling stops.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Assess the chest pain and vital signs while calmly stating the expectation.
Delay the assessment until the client stops shouting to avoid reinforcing the behavior.
Notify the provider of the chest pain before going to assess the client.
Give the prescribed PRN pain medication, then reassess the chest pain.
optionRationales: Correct. New chest pain rated 8/10 could signal a serious physiologic problem, so the nurse assesses right away while calmly stating the behavioral expectation. Limits never require withholding essential care.
Incorrect. Avoiding reinforcement of behavior is a real goal, but delaying assessment of new chest pain risks missing a life-threatening problem.
Incorrect. The provider will likely need to know, but the nurse should first gather pain and vital-sign data to report.
Incorrect. Pain relief matters, but treating new chest pain before assessing it may mask a cardiac problem and skips needed data.
questions.rationale: Setting limits never requires withholding essential assessment or treatment. New chest pain could signal a serious physiologic problem, so the nurse assesses immediately while calmly stating the behavioral expectation. A behavioral label must not obscure pain, medical instability, or medication effects. After the situation is safe, the team can coordinate a consistent plan for the behavior.
questions.takeaway: Limits and essential care happen together; never withhold assessment to manage behavior.
questions.hintContent: Which symptom could be life-threatening regardless of the behavior?
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the immediate need and the action that addresses it before longer-term steps.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A client with a new ileostomy has a goal of improved self-concept. Which documentation entry provides the best evidence of progress toward that goal?
options: “Self-esteem has improved significantly since admission, based on nursing judgment.”
“Client named two personal strengths and emptied the pouch with coaching.”
“Client appears happier and more cheerful today than on the prior shift.”
“Client stated, ‘I feel better about how I look with the pouch now.’”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Nursing judgment matters, but this is a conclusion without the observable evidence behind it.

Correct. Naming strengths and performing pouch care with coaching are specific, observable behaviors showing both self-perception and engagement in care, the strongest evidence of self-concept progress.
Incorrect. Mood observations are useful, but “appears happier” is subjective and does not show specific self-concept behaviors.
Incorrect. The client’s own words are meaningful evidence, but a single statement is stronger when paired with observable behavior and participation in care.
questions.rationale: Progress in self-concept is evaluated through the client’s experience together with specific behavior, participation, coping, safety, and function. Naming strengths and performing a chosen care task with coaching are observable outcomes. Broad conclusions such as “self-esteem improved” do not show the evidence behind them. A client saying they feel better is meaningful, but it should be considered alongside function and safety.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate self-concept with specific, observable participation and function.
questions.hintContent: Which entry would let another nurse see exactly what the client did?
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A client’s treatment plan includes dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) with a licensed therapist. In the evening, the client tells the nurse, “I am so upset after that phone call that I cannot calm down.” The client denies thoughts of harming self or others. Which nursing action best fits the plan?
options: Hold a full DBT session tonight to speed up the client’s progress.
Offer a prescribed PRN anxiolytic to help the client calm down.
Coach the client to use a distress-tolerance skill practiced in therapy.
Encourage the client to discuss the phone call at the next therapy session.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Supporting DBT is appropriate, but delivering a full session is outside the nurse’s role; trained therapists provide the therapy.
Incorrect. A PRN may be appropriate if distress continues, but the least restrictive step is to coach a coping skill the client already has.
Correct. Nurses support the plan by coaching skills learned in therapy. Distress tolerance fits acute upset in a client without safety concerns and is less restrictive than medication.
Incorrect. Bringing the event to therapy is useful, but the client needs help calming down now, not only later.
questions.rationale: DBT includes skills such as mindfulness, emotion regulation, and distress tolerance. Nurses support the treatment plan by reinforcing skills the client has learned, while trained clinicians deliver the full therapy. A brief supportive coaching moment should not be presented as a specialist session. Because the client denies thoughts of harm, coaching is appropriate, but the nurse continues to monitor safety.
questions.takeaway: Reinforce the client’s therapy skills within the plan rather than replacing or expanding the therapy.
questions.hintContent: DBT skills include distress tolerance; consider the nurse’s role in reinforcing them.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the specific cues in the scenario to compare all options; choose the one that best meets the stated goal.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A newly admitted client says, “The last time I was in the hospital, nobody told me anything.” Which nursing actions build trust? Select all that apply.
options: State your role and return at 1500 to recheck pain, as promised.
Tell the client, “You will definitely feel better by tomorrow.”
Explain each procedure before beginning it.
Share detailed stories about your own hospital experiences to build rapport.
Let the client know promptly when the plan of care changes.
Promise to keep everything the client says secret, including safety concerns.
optionRationales: Correct. Clarity about your role and reliable follow-through communicate respect and build trust.
Incorrect. A promise outside the nurse’s control is false reassurance that can damage credibility.
Correct. Explaining care before acting supports understanding and control.
Incorrect. Excessive self-disclosure shifts the focus away from the client.
Correct. Honest updates prevent the sense of being left uninformed.
Incorrect. Safety information must be shared with the team, so this promise cannot be kept.
questions.rationale: Trust grows through honest, consistent action: being clear about your role, explaining care, and following through on commitments. Telling the client when plans change prevents the experience the client described. False reassurance, excessive personal disclosure, and promises outside the nurse’s control undermine the therapeutic relationship. Confidentiality is protected according to policy, but safety concerns must be shared with the team.
questions.takeaway: Build trust through honest explanation and reliable follow-through, not promises you cannot keep.
questions.hintContent: Can the nurse truthfully keep each promise or statement?
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: Before discharge, the nurse teaches the family of a client recovering from a stroke who was the household’s main earner and now needs help with his daily activities. Which family statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “We will let him make the decisions he is able to make, like planning meals.”
“We should do everything for him so he does not get frustrated.”
“We will ask him which tasks he wants to keep doing himself.”
“If he says he feels fine, we do not need to watch for changes in mood.”
“Caring for him is a lot, so we will ask social work about respite options.”
“We will tell him to stop talking about his old job so he accepts the change.”
optionRationales: Correct. Supporting decisions within his ability preserves autonomy and role.
Incorrect. Taking over every task undermines self-efficacy and independence.
Correct. Asking his priorities keeps goals client-centered.
Incorrect. Mood and coping still need monitoring even when he says he feels fine.
Correct. Recognizing caregiver strain and seeking resources supports a sustainable plan.
Incorrect. Silencing his grief over a lost role dismisses the loss and may increase distress.
questions.rationale: Families support self-concept by preserving the client’s choices, valued roles, and participation at his current ability. Asking what he wants to keep doing keeps goals individualized. Caregivers may be willing but need skills, respite, or resources, so recognizing strain is appropriate. Taking over every task, ignoring mood, or silencing talk about a lost role works against adaptation.
questions.takeaway: Teach families to preserve choices and roles, watch mood, and seek support for caregiver strain.
questions.hintContent: Look for statements that keep him participating and keep the family supported.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently against the client’s findings and the stated goal; do not assume a fixed number of correct choices.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43
